channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Colorado confirms foreign actors changed settings, silenced alarms and altered pumping at two small water systems
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Colorado’s Governor’s office said on 18 September that foreign actors breached two small, privately owned drinking-water providers in late August, changing equipment settings, disabling alarms and remote access, and altering pumping cycles. The state says the disruptions were brief, the providers corrected them and alerted the state, and there was no known effect on treatment, water quality or public safety. The office cannot confirm which actors were involved, though it points to a known Iranian-backed campaign against water and wastewater systems; The FBI declined to comment, and Denver Water says its own systems were evaluated and are unaffected. Why this matters: the national campaign against internet-exposed water controllers now has hands-on process tampering confirmed by a state government rather than inferred. Each utility serves fewer than 200 people — and at that size, the alarm the intruders switched off is often the only operator on shift. - Colorado Governor’s office statement, reported by Reuters, AP, Axios Denver, the Denver Post, KRDO and SecurityWeek; context from CISA, FBI, EPA and NSA advisory AA26-097A - Intrusions late Aug 2026; disclosed 18 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The Coast Guard cleared the boarded supertanker to resume trading — after finding evidence of a malicious actor aboard
item.category: Incident — confirmed malicious cyber activity aboard two US-bound tankers; no confirmed operational disruption; attribution unresolved
item.description: US Coast Guard and FBI personnel boarded two Texas-bound oil tankers in late August after indications that the vessels’ networks had been breached during the voyage. Rear Adm. Amy Grable, who commands Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News that reviewing the IT and other onboard systems of the Liberian-flagged crude carrier VL Prosperity did turn up evidence of a malicious cyber actor, but that nothing found suggested the ship was unsafe to operate. Iranian state media claims the intrusion reached the engine room — slowing coolant flow, raising engine speed, interfering with fuel delivery and cutting communications for about 30 hours — and those claims remain unverified; the Coast Guard has not attributed the incident to Iran. The vessel has since been cleared to resume normal operations, with a final investigation report still outstanding. The detail worth sitting with is Grable’s: this was one of an estimated 40–50 cyber missions the Coast Guard’s Cyber Protection Team carried out in the past year. - US Coast Guard Cyber Command via CBS News; Wall Street Journal; reported by SecurityWeek, The Record, Industrial Cyber, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and gCaptain - Boardings late Aug 2026; reported 15–18 Sep 2026; vessel cleared, reported 18–19 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] A US-loaded LNG carrier turned away from its discharge port after losing control systems — and the crew say the valves were being driven from somewhere else
item.category: Incident — confirmed control-system malfunction aboard an LNG carrier; crew claim cyber manipulation of pressure and relief valves, cause not established
item.description: The Liberia-flagged LNG carrier Vivit Africa, loaded at Cameron LNG in Louisiana and bound for Rovigo, Italy, lost access to some internal control systems as it approached the Adriatic in early September. The Italian Coast Guard confirmed it assisted the vessel after the master reported a malfunction affecting cargo-parameter monitoring; the ship never discharged and instead sailed for Algeciras, Spain. Crew members separately told the trade press that attackers took temporary control of steam pressure and safety valve systems near Gibraltar and later of tank pressure controls and relief valves in the Adriatic. Officials have not established a cause and no attribution has been offered. For OT defenders the value here is the shape of the claim, not its verdict: the systems described are the ones that keep a cargo inside its safe envelope, and they are reachable from the same integrated automation network as the monitoring that failed. - Italian Coast Guard statement via Reuters, carried by gCaptain and Insurance Journal; crew accounts reported by Splash247; vessel and charter details via Bloomberg - Incident early Sep 2026; reported 18–19 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A cyberattack stopped container handling at Tanjung Pelepas — and the restart ran on paper and manual gate-ins
item.category: Incident — confirmed cyberattack on terminal operating systems; container handling suspended at one of the world’s largest transhipment hubs
item.description: The Port of Tanjung Pelepas in Malaysia detected a cyber incident affecting its terminal operating systems late on 9 September and suspended container-handling operations as a precaution. A phased restart began the following day, with some export gate-ins processed manually while systems were recovered; the operator says container operations have since resumed. PTP is an MMC Group and APM Terminals joint venture that moved 14.03 million TEU in 2025, which puts it among the largest transhipment hubs anywhere. For OT defenders this is the cleanest recent example of the pattern that actually causes industrial downtime: the attack did not need to reach a crane PLC or a straddle carrier to stop the boxes moving — taking out the system that decides where every container goes was sufficient. - Port of Tanjung Pelepas spokesperson statement, reported by WorldCargo News - Incident detected 9 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Settra hit a manufacturer, cleared the logs and disabled recovery — and the responders could not establish how it got in
item.category: Incident — Settra ransomware at a manufacturer; VPN access, RMM persistence, BYOVD evasion, logs cleared; no OT impact stated
item.description: Huntress detailed a September intrusion at a manufacturing company by the newly identified Settra ransomware variant, alongside a July case at a retail and consumer-services firm. In the manufacturing case the responders observed a vulnerable signed driver used to disable security controls, encryption, clearing of Windows event logs and disabling of recovery options — and were not able to establish the method of initial access. In the July case at the other firm they found the MeshAgent remote monitoring tool used for persistence. No OT impact was reported, and that is precisely the point worth making to a plant manager: the chain contains no industrial protocol, no controller exploit and no ICS knowledge, yet it lands on the systems production depends on. - Huntress research, reported by Cybersecurity Dive - Published 18 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CenterPoint Energy confirms a breach through an external-facing system — service unaffected, but the utility found out from a leak post
item.category: Incident — utility breach confirmed via SEC 8-K; customer data taken through an external-facing system; electric and gas delivery not impacted
item.description: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based electric and gas utility, filed an 8-K on 14 September confirming it became aware of a third-party post claiming to hold CenterPoint customer data, and that an unauthorised party did obtain personal information through one of its external-facing systems. The company states that delivery of electric and gas service was not impacted. The poster claims roughly 7.5 million records including names, account and billing data, driver’s licence numbers and partial Social Security numbers; CenterPoint has not confirmed that figure or the authenticity of the dataset. From an OT standpoint this is an IT-side breach with no operational consequence — but the sequence is the part worth noting internally: the utility learned of it from a leak post rather than from its own detection. - CenterPoint Energy SEC Form 8-K, reported by The Record, SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - 8-K filed 14 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Twelve flaws in a Siemens edge processing box chain to root — the device that sits between your PROFINET segment and everything else
item.category: Research — Nozomi Networks Labs: 12 vulnerabilities in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 local processing engine; chainable to root
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its research on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 Local Processing Engine, identifying twelve vulnerabilities in firmware below V4.0 HF0, with three more affecting other configurations including the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client. The reported issue classes cover privilege escalation, path traversal, authentication bypass, command injection and buffer overflows, several of which chain to root-level control — which on this class of device means telemetry manipulation, alarm suppression and a foothold for attacks against the OT network behind it. Siemens has no fix for some of the findings; the published workarounds are restricting access and disabling the PROFINET DCP service. One presentational note: the identifiers attached to this research are 2025-series CVEs appearing in a September 2026 write-up, which is legitimate — Siemens and CISA advisory activity for this device dates back to 2025 — but it means part of this is a fuller public account of older findings rather than wholly new disclosure. Check the identifiers against Siemens ProductCERT before raising a change record. - Nozomi Networks Labs research, reported by Industrial Cyber; verify identifiers against Siemens ProductCERT - Published 18 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] A 720-page incident-response framework just went free — and one of its chapters is about control systems
item.description: SANS published Dynamic Incident Response: A Framework for Security Teams by SANS Fellow Joshua Wright on 15 September, the first substantial rebuild of the SANS incident-response framework in roughly twenty years. It is 720 pages across twenty chapters, free in every digital format under a Creative Commons licence, and the model it introduces — DAIR, a Dynamic Approach to Incident Response — aligns to NIST guidance and the Cybersecurity Framework while abandoning the assumption that response proceeds through neat sequential phases. Three chapters are contributed: Dean Parsons on operational technology and control systems, Megan Roddie-Fonseca on cloud, Ryan Chapman on ransomware and extortion. For OT teams the value is less the model than the availability: there is now a current, citable, no-cost reference with a control-systems chapter that you can put in front of a plant manager, an engineering lead or a procurement reviewer without a licence conversation. - SANS Institute announcement; book available free at dynamicincidentresponse.com - Published 15 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Manufacturing ransomware is up 40% and the victim has moved to mid-market Europe — which changes who your supplier risk is
item.category: Report — Black Kite: 1,183 manufacturing ransomware victims through July 2026, up ~40%; European victims up 85%; half from crews under two years old
item.description: Black Kite counted 1,183 new manufacturing ransomware victims between January and July 2026, a rise of roughly 40% on the same period in 2025, and 5,237 disclosed victims since January 2023. Half of this year’s attacks came from groups that did not exist two years ago; one new crew alone accounted for 12% of them. The geography moved sharply: European victims rose 85% — Germany 77, Italy 57, the UK 43, France 40 — while US volume was flat, dropping the US share from 52% to 35%. For anyone running a supply-chain risk programme, the practical consequence is that your exposure has shifted toward mid-market European suppliers who are less likely to have an OT security programme, a tested recovery plan, or the ability to tell you quickly that they are down. - Black Kite 2026 Manufacturing & Distribution Ransomware Report, reported by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive and Industrial Cyber - Published 17 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The box that decides which VLAN a device lands in can be taken by an unauthenticated request — and it is being taken
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-76460, CVSS 10.0, Cisco Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC; exploited as a zero-day, no workaround, in KEV
item.description: Cisco disclosed a maximum-severity authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and the ISE Passive Identity Connector, tracked as CVE-2026-76460 at CVSS 10.0, caused by insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint. An unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the web management interface and gain unauthorised access to the device. Cisco says it was exploited as a zero-day; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September, now passed. There is no workaround — upgrading is the only remediation, with fixes in ISE 3.5 P4, 3.4 P7, 3.3 P12, 3.2 P11 and 3.1 P12. For industrial sites, ISE is frequently the thing enforcing which devices land on which VLAN, including the boundary between enterprise and plant. Whoever holds ISE can rewrite that boundary without touching a switch, a firewall or a controller. - Cisco security advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, reported by SecurityWeek, CyberScoop, BleepingComputer and The Hacker News - Disclosed and added to KEV 16 Sep 2026; federal deadline 19 Sep 2026, now passed — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Two SonicWall SMA1000 flaws chain to unauthenticated code execution — and where compromise is suspected the advice is to reimage and rotate
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-83548 (CVSS 10.0 pre-auth SSRF) and CVE-2026-83549 (CVSS 7.8 post-auth OS command injection), SonicWall SMA1000; chained and exploited in the wild, both in KEV
item.description: SonicWall disclosed two flaws in SMA1000 secure remote-access appliances on 1 September: a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Work Place interface at CVSS 10.0, and a post-authentication OS command injection in the Appliance Management Console at CVSS 7.8. Rapid7 reports the pair chain to unauthenticated remote code execution on an appliance that is normally internet-facing by design. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September. SonicWall published no indicators of compromise and told customers to contact support to review appliances for signs of intrusion and, where compromise is suspected, to re-image or redeploy, rotate all credentials and reset TOTP tokens — which tells you what the vendor thinks the realistic post-exploitation state is. This is the fifth KEV-listed SMA1000 defect since December 2025, and ransomware crews including INC and Akira have repeatedly used SonicWall gear as an entry point into environments that include plant networks. - SonicWall advisory, Rapid7 analysis and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, reported by CyberScoop - Disclosed 1 Sep 2026; KEV additions 2 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Siemens protection relays leak enough to calculate a valid session ID — authentication bypassed on substation feeder protection
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-62645, CVSS v3.1 9.8 / v4.0 9.3, Siemens Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays below V2.70; CISA ICSA-26-258-05; automatable, no known exploitation
item.description: Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 covers nine newly assigned 2026 vulnerabilities in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays running firmware below V2.70, alongside several older third-party identifiers carried in the same advisory. The most serious, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4.0 9.3, exposes enough information through the device web interface for an unauthenticated network attacker to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication entirely. The set also includes a low-entropy session token, an HTTP resource-exhaustion denial of service that reboots the device, and a memory-corruption issue in firmware-update mode. CISA republished it as ICSA-26-258-05 on 15 September and its own SSVC scoring marks the flaw automatable. No exploitation has been reported. This is the most sector-specific item on the page for electric utilities: these are feeder protection relays, and a relay that can be reconfigured or rebooted is a protection-system problem, not an IT one. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-142885 and CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-05; corroborated by SecurityWeek ICS Patch Tuesday coverage - Siemens advisory 8 Sep 2026; CISA advisory 15 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] An authentication-algorithm flaw in Modicon M580 — including the Safety variant — when the project runs at a lower application level
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-3869, CVSS v4.0 9.2, Schneider Electric Modicon M580 and M580 Safety; SEVD-2026-251-04; no known exploitation
item.description: Schneider Electric’s 8 September advisory SEVD-2026-251-04 discloses CVE-2026-3869, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm (CWE-303) in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, carrying CVSS v4.0 9.2. The condition applies when a project with a lower application level is running: all M580 below application level 4.00 and all M580 Safety below 4.20 are affected, with potential loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability of the controller. No CVSS v3.1 score has been published. CISA’s enrichment records exploitation as none and automatable as no, and the EPSS score is very low. The detail that matters operationally is the application-level condition: many sites are running older project files on newer firmware without realising that the authentication behaviour follows the project, not the controller. - Schneider Electric advisory SEVD-2026-251-04 and the CVE record for CVE-2026-3869; corroborated by SecurityWeek ICS Patch Tuesday coverage - Schneider advisory 8 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The OEM maintenance tunnel runs commands as root, survives reboots, and keeps working normally while it does
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-75925, CVSS v3.1 9.6, IXON VPN Client below 1.4.7; unauthenticated CRLF injection to root/SYSTEM; CISA ICSA-26-246-02
item.description: CISA republished IXON’s advisory as ICSA-26-246-02. The IXON VPN Client’s local configuration interface accepts changes without authenticating the requester, and values written to a configuration file consumed by a privileged subprocess are not neutralised for line endings. Chained, an attacker can inject additional directives and execute commands as root on Linux or SYSTEM on Windows, tracked as CVE-2026-75925 at CVSS v3.1 9.6. The two details that make this an OT problem rather than an endpoint problem: the injected configuration persists across reboots, and the VPN carries on working normally afterwards, so there is no user-visible sign. CISA lists the affected sectors as commercial facilities, critical manufacturing, energy, information technology, and water and wastewater — which is a fair description of everywhere an OEM installs a remote-maintenance tunnel. - CISA advisory ICSA-26-246-02, republishing the IXON vendor advisory - IXON advisory 5 Aug 2026; CISA republication 3 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The management server for a SCADA product takes privileged commands without asking who you are — and its SMS gateway will text anyone
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-73807, CVSS v3.1 9.8, mySCADA myPRO Manager V2.1 and earlier; CISA ICSA-26-258-03; no known exploitation
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-258-03 on 15 September covering two flaws in mySCADA myPRO Manager, the component that administers myPRO SCADA deployments. The serious one, CVE-2026-73807 at CVSS v3.1 9.8, is a missing authorisation check on the command API: privileged management functions can be reached by an unauthenticated caller with network access to the manager. The second, CVE-2026-82567 at 6.3, is an HTTP endpoint on the notification gateway that will send arbitrary SMS messages through an attached GSM modem without authentication. Everything at V2.1 and earlier is affected and V2.2 carries the fix. No exploitation has been reported. This vendor is popular with small water, district heating and building-automation operators — the sites least likely to know the manager is internet-reachable, and the ones where the SMS gateway is the alarm system. - CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-03 and mySCADA vendor release notes; CVE records corroborated via NVD enrichment data - CISA advisory 15 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Two hard-coded keys in shipboard automation — one in the update controller that decides what software a vessel runs
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-81855 (CVSS 9.1) and CVE-2026-78225 (CVSS v3.1 9.0 / v4.0 9.5), Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard 5.07.0923.01; CISA ICSA-26-258-02; no known exploitation
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-258-02 on 15 September covering two hard-coded cryptographic keys in Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard, the onboard platform layer used with the vendor’s vessel automation products. CVE-2026-78225 is a fixed server key in the deployer-ng Update Controller: because the key never changes and is not held in secure storage, anyone able to reach or influence that component could decode protected traffic, sign certificates or forge control messages. CVE-2026-81855 is a hard-coded client authentication key in the robot testing framework component, letting an attacker impersonate a legitimate client. Wärtsilä says the flaws are not exploitable when the product is installed as recommended and has produced a patch available on request. No exploitation has been reported. Coming in the same week as two vessel incidents on this page, the location matters more than the scores: the update path is how software gets onto a ship that is at sea for weeks. - CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-02 and Wärtsilä security notice; CVE records corroborated via NVD enrichment data - CISA advisory 15 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The block password that protects your control program is checked by the program checking it — and that check can be patched in memory
item.category: Advisory — CVE-2026-15688, CVSS v3.1 8.8 / v4.0 9.2, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, all versions; CISA ICSA-26-260-02; local attack, no known exploitation
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-260-02 on 17 September covering CVE-2026-15688 in Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and the Motion Control Settings software packaged with it. The weakness is CWE-303, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm: a local attacker who runs the engineering software and modifies part of the executable module in memory can authenticate with an invalid block password, then view, tamper with, destroy or delete the protected control programs. All versions are affected. Mitsubishi’s vector is local with low privileges, and CISA scores it 8.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.2 under v4.0; no exploitation has been reported. The practical reading is blunt: block passwords are widely treated as intellectual-property and safety protection for logic, and this says they are a speed bump for anyone who already has the engineering workstation. - CISA advisory ICSA-26-260-02 and Mitsubishi Electric PSIRT bulletin; CVE record corroborated via NVD enrichment data - CISA advisory 17 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A kernel bug in the box that aggregates your plant data — any workload already on the node can become root
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICSA-26-260-06 / ABB: Linux kernel flaw in Ability Edgenius lets a local account or container workload reach root on the edge node
item.description: ABB Ability Edgenius ships a Linux kernel carrying CVE-2026-31431, an incorrect in-place operation in the kernel’s algif_aead cryptographic interface where source and destination mappings differ. A locally authenticated user — or a container workload already running on the node — can invoke that interface, trigger the faulty memory handling and escalate to root, which means arbitrary code execution, full control of the node, or making it unavailable. CVSS v3.1 7.8, CVSS v4.0 7.3. ABB fixed it in Edgenius 3.2.4.1 and CISA republished the advisory on 17 September. It is not remotely exploitable on its own, and that is exactly how it should be read rather than filed: Edgenius is a containerised edge platform that aggregates process data and carries it northbound, so it habitually sits with one interface on the plant network and one facing the enterprise or cloud. This flaw converts “an app on the edge box misbehaved” into “the edge box belongs to someone else.” - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-260-06, republishing ABB’s PSIRT advisory - Published 17 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The grid supply-chain order names RTUs, PLCs and safety systems — and lets DOE make you isolate or replace gear already installed
item.category: Policy — Executive Order 14420: national emergency on foreign-produced bulk-power system equipment; ICS explicitly in scope; DOE implementing regulations due within 120 days
item.description: Executive Order 14420, signed 26 August, declares a national emergency over foreign-produced bulk-power system equipment and prohibits acquiring, importing, transferring or installing such equipment tied to designated entities where the transaction was initiated after that date. Scope is transmission at 69 kV and above — local distribution is explicitly excluded — and covers transformers, inverters, generators and battery storage and industrial control systems: remote terminal units, programmable logic controllers and safety systems, together with associated firmware, software and remote-access capability. For equipment already installed, DOE can require operators to identify, isolate, monitor, secure, disconnect or replace components, and may publish a pre-qualified vendor list and negotiate mitigation agreements. No country is named in the order. The order gives DOE 120 days to publish implementing regulations, and until those rules land no individual transaction is formally prohibited — so the scope being written this autumn decides how expensive the fleet-level question becomes. - Executive Order 14420 (White House), reported by SecurityWeek - Order signed 26 Aug 2026; reported 27 Aug 2026; DOE implementing regulations due within 120 days — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six national agencies published the Active Directory playbook — and for most plants that directory is the shortest route from the office to the control room
item.category: Guidance — ASD, CISA, NSA, CCCS, NCSC-NZ and NCSC-UK: detecting and mitigating 17 Active Directory compromise techniques
item.description: Six national cyber agencies — Australia’s ASD, CISA, NSA, Canada’s CCCS, New Zealand’s NCSC and the UK’s NCSC — published joint guidance on 16 September covering the seventeen techniques adversaries most commonly use to compromise Microsoft Active Directory, with detection methods and hardening recommendations for each. The list runs from Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting and password spraying through unconstrained delegation, AD Certificate Services abuse, DCSync and NTDS.dit extraction to golden and silver tickets, golden SAML, Entra Connect compromise, SID history abuse and shadow credentials. There is nothing OT-specific in it, which is exactly why it belongs on this page: in most plants the engineering workstations, historians and HMIs are domain-joined, and every OT-impacting ransomware case on this dashboard ran through identity rather than through an industrial protocol. - Joint guidance from ASD, CISA, NSA, CCCS, NCSC-NZ and NCSC-UK, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 16 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s answer to living-off-the-land: put things on the network that nobody has any legitimate reason to touch
item.description: CISA published guidance on 16 September on deploying cyber decoys — tripwires, breadcrumbs and honeytokens — inside internal networks and systems, explicitly framed around adversaries who use stolen valid accounts, built-in administrative utilities and other living-off-the-land techniques that produce no malware to detect. The logic is simple and unusually well suited to OT: a decoy credential, API key, document, database record or cloud token has no role in normal operations, so any interaction with one is a high-fidelity alert rather than another entry in a queue. The guide maps decoy placement to MITRE Engage and ATT&CK and walks through planning, implementation and refinement at low complexity. The part worth flagging to budget-constrained plants: CISA tells organisations to repurpose EDR, identity and data-loss-prevention tooling they already own to deploy and monitor decoys, not to buy a deception platform. - CISA guidance, corroborated by CyberScoop and Industrial Cyber reporting - Published 16 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting is live — 24 hours to tell ENISA about an actively exploited flaw, including in products already sold
item.category: Regulation — EU Cyber Resilience Act Article 14 reporting live since 11 September 2026; 24-hour early warning; applies to products already on the market
item.description: From 11 September, the Cyber Resilience Act’s Article 14 reporting obligations are mandatory. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents to ENISA and the relevant national CSIRT on a staged clock: early warning within 24 hours, technical notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days for an exploited vulnerability or one month for a severe incident. ENISA’s CRA Single Reporting Platform went live the same day. The detail that matters for OT is that this bites on products already on the market, not only new ones, and reaches OT vendors, embedded and IoT makers, networking suppliers and system integrators who substantially modify products. Full manufacturer conformity obligations follow in December 2027. - European Commission CRA reporting guidance and the ENISA Single Reporting Platform; corroborated by legal-sector analysis published the same day - Obligations effective 11 Sep 2026; conformity obligations from Dec 2027 — verified 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] FERC approved a rewritten substation physical-security standard — and the new risk assessment now has to look over the fence at the substation next door
item.category: Regulation — FERC approves NERC Reliability Standard CIP-014-4 (Physical Security), Docket RD26-9-000; order issued 10 September 2026, published 15 September 2026; effective 1 October 2028
item.description: FERC approved NERC Reliability Standard CIP-014-4 on 10 September, published in the Federal Register on 15 September. The rewrite does not widen which substations are in scope; it tightens how transmission owners prove the ones they picked are the right ones. The applicable-facility list must be reviewed at least every 36 months and must include stations planned to be in service within that window. A new Requirement R2 makes owners identify proximate bulk electric system stations and substations within 1,500 feet, fence line to fence line, irrespective of ownership, and feed them into the risk assessment. The methodology itself becomes prescriptive: documented, technically justified thresholds for instability, uncontrolled separation and cascading, and steady-state and dynamic simulations run against at least one peak and one off-peak load case. The single 36-month assessment cycle replaces today’s split 30/60-month cadence, which shortens the maximum re-look for owners who previously found nothing critical from five years to three. CIP-014-3 retires immediately before the new standard takes effect on 1 October 2028. - FERC order approving Reliability Standard CIP-014-4, Docket RD26-9-000, Federal Register 91 FR 58430; corroborated by law-firm and trade-press analysis - Order issued 10 Sep 2026; published 15 Sep 2026; standard effective 1 Oct 2028 — verified 21 Sep 2026
